claim: Foxb1-expressing neurons occur in the dorsal premammillary nucleus (PMd) and further rostrally in the parvafox nucleus, a longitudinal cluster of neurons in the lateral hypothalamus of rodents.
source: Foxb1 -expressing neurons occur in the dorsal premammillary nucleus (PMd) and further rostrally in the parvafox nucleus, a longitudinal cluster of neurons in the lateral hypothalamus of rodents.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing the anatomical location of Foxb1-expressing neurons.

claim: The descending projection of Foxb1+ neurons end in the dorsolateral part of the periaqueductal gray (dlPAG).
source: The descending projection of these Foxb1+ neurons end in the dorsolateral part of the periaqueductal gray (dlPAG).
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing the projection target of Foxb1+ neurons.

claim: hM3Dq-mediated, global Foxb1+ neuron excitation activates respiration in whole-body barometric plethysmography.
source: Our results show that in whole-body barometric plethysmography, hM3Dq-mediated, global Foxb1+ neuron excitation activates respiration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-body plethysmography experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Time-resolved optogenetic gain-of-function manipulation of the terminal endings of Foxb1+ neurons in the rostral third of the dlPAG leads to abrupt immobility.
source: Time-resolved optogenetic gain-of-function manipulation of the terminal endings of Foxb1+ neurons in the rostral third of the dlPAG leads to abrupt immobility and bradycardia.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Time-resolved optogenetic gain-of-function manipulation of the terminal endings of Foxb1+ neurons in the rostral third of the dlPAG leads to bradycardia.
source: Time-resolved optogenetic gain-of-function manipulation of the terminal endings of Foxb1+ neurons in the rostral third of the dlPAG leads to abrupt immobility and bradycardia.
evidence: This claim is supported by cardiovascular telemetry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of Foxb1+ cell bodies and ChR2-mediated excitation of their axonal endings in the dlPAG led to a phenotypical presentation congruent with a 'freezing-like' situation during innate defensive behavior.
source: Chemogenetic activation of Foxb1+ cell bodies and ChR2-mediated excitation of their axonal endings in the dlPAG led to a phenotypical presentation congruent with a 'freezing-like' situation during innate defensive behavior.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the combined chemogenetic and optogenetic experimental data.

claim: One neuronal migratory stream expressing Foxb1 forms most of the mamillary body during hypothalamic development.
source: During hypothalamic development, two neuronal migratory streams expressing the transcription factor Foxb1 form the nuclei of the mamillary region as well as one nucleus of the lateral hypothalamus (LHA). One of these streams forms most of the mamillary body while the other forms the dorsal premammillary nucleus (PMd) and the Foxb1-expressing neurons of the parvafox nucleus (parvafoxFoxb1) in the LHA (Alvarez-Bolado et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Alvarez-Bolado et al., 2000).

claim: One neuronal migratory stream expressing Foxb1 forms the dorsal premammillary nucleus (PMd) and the Foxb1-expressing neurons of the parvafox nucleus (parvafoxFoxb1) in the LHA.
source: During hypothalamic development, two neuronal migratory streams expressing the transcription factor Foxb1 form the nuclei of the mamillary region as well as one nucleus of the lateral hypothalamus (LHA). One of these streams forms most of the mamillary body while the other forms the dorsal premammillary nucleus (PMd) and the Foxb1-expressing neurons of the parvafox nucleus (parvafoxFoxb1) in the LHA (Alvarez-Bolado et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Alvarez-Bolado et al., 2000).

claim: The ventrolateral part of the PMd (vlPMd) projects to the dorsolateral periaqueductal gray (dlPAG).
source: The ventrolateral part of the PMd (vlPMd) projects to the dorsolateral periaqueductal gray (dlPAG; Canteras and Swanson, 1992) while the parvafoxFoxb1 axon terminals occupy a region straddling the dlPAG and the lPAG (Bilella et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Canteras and Swanson, 1992).

claim: The parvafoxFoxb1 axon terminals occupy a region straddling the dlPAG and the lPAG.
source: The ventrolateral part of the PMd (vlPMd) projects to the dorsolateral periaqueductal gray (dlPAG; Canteras and Swanson, 1992) while the parvafoxFoxb1 axon terminals occupy a region straddling the dlPAG and the lPAG (Bilella et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Bilella et al., 2016).

claim: The dlPAG is associated with innate defensive responses like 'freezing' and escape behavior.
source: Solid evidence indicates that the dlPAG is associated with innate defensive responses like 'freezing' and escape behavior (Canteras and Goto, 1999; Vianna et al., 2001; Bittencourt et al., 2004; Deng et al., 2016; Kunwar et al., 2015; Souza and Carobrez, 2016; Evans et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The dlPAG receives afferences from neurons of the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) expressing steroidogenic factor 1 (SF1+).
source: In addition to inputs from Foxb1+ cells of the hypothalamus, the dlPAG also receives afferences from neurons of the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) expressing steroidogenic factor 1 (SF1+).
evidence: This is a statement about anatomical connectivity based on established knowledge.

claim: Optogenetic activation of SF1+ cell bodies in the VMH leads to immobility.
source: The optogenetic activation of their cell bodies in the VMH (Kunwar et al., 2015) and of their terminal endings in the dlPAG (Wang et al., 2015a) leads to immobility.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Kunwar et al., 2015).

claim: Optogenetic activation of SF1+ terminal endings in the dlPAG leads to immobility.
source: The optogenetic activation of their cell bodies in the VMH (Kunwar et al., 2015) and of their terminal endings in the dlPAG (Wang et al., 2015a) leads to immobility.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Wang et al., 2015a).

claim: As the stimulation intensity of SF1+ neurons increases, immobility is followed by bursts of activity (running and jumping).
source: As the stimulation intensity increases, immobility is followed by bursts of activity (running and jumping; Kunwar et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Kunwar et al., 2015).

claim: The behavioral change from immobility to bursts of activity is ascribed to the co-activation of another axon collateral of the SF1+ neurons, innervating the anterior hypothalamic nucleus (AHN).
source: This behavioral change is ascribed to the co-activation of another axon collateral of the SF1+ neurons, innervating the anterior hypothalamic nucleus (AHN; Wang et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Wang et al., 2015a).

claim: Increasing the intensity of the stimulation of SF1+ cell bodies in the VMH leads to a change of the cardiovascular responses from tachycardia to bradycardia as animals remain immobile.
source: As animals remain immobile, increasing the intensity of the stimulation of SF1+ cell bodies in the VMH leads to a change of the cardiovascular responses from tachycardia to bradycardia (Wang et al., 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Wang et al., 2015b).

claim: The dlPAG receives afferences from medially located glutamatergic neurons of the superior colliculus (mSC).
source: The third afference to the dlPAG (Schenberg et al., 2005) stems from medially located glutamatergic neurons of the superior colliculus (mSC), which is responsive to innately aversive looming stimuli (Evans et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Schenberg et al., 2005; Evans et al., 2018).

claim: mSC neurons are responsive to innately aversive looming stimuli.
source: The third afference to the dlPAG (Schenberg et al., 2005) stems from medially located glutamatergic neurons of the superior colliculus (mSC), which is responsive to innately aversive looming stimuli (Evans et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Evans et al., 2018).

claim: mSC neurons integrate threat evidence and pass the information through a synaptic threshold to the glutamatergic dlPAG neurons that initiate escape.
source: mSC neurons integrate threat evidence and pass the information through a synaptic threshold to the glutamatergic dlPAG neurons that initiate escape (Evans et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Evans et al., 2018).

claim: The activation of hM3Dq expressed in the parvafoxFoxb1 by intraperitoneal clozapine or CNO injection led to changes in several parameters of respiration consistent with an increased respiratory effort.
source: The activation of the hM3Dq (activating DREADD receptors) expressed in the parvafoxFoxb1 by intraperitoneal clozapine or CNO injection led to changes in several parameters of respiration consistent with an increased respiratory effort Figure 2; breaths per minute (BPM), F(2,26)=6.061, p=0.00691, g=; inspiratory time (IT), F(2,26) = 5.831, p=0.00809; total time (TT) F(2,26)=4.655, p=0.01973; minute volume adjusted for bodyweight (MVadjPerGram), F(2,26)=3.998, p=0.03265; peak inspiratory flow (PIFadj), F(2,26) = 4.284, p=0.03439; all reported results are obtained by a 3x3 mixed-design ANOVA for the 'Condition' factor, p values are Huynh-Feldt sphericity corrected.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from whole-body plethysmography experiments, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: A significant increase in BPM was observed within saline, clozapine and CNO injected hM3Dq animals.
source: Namely, we observed a significant increase in three parameters within saline, clozapine and CNO injected hM3Dq animals: (1) BPM (Figure 2a–I; saline vs. clozapine: t(5) = –3.199, p=0.024, g = –1.380 (large); saline vs. CNO: t(5) = –2.916, p=0.033, g = –1.192(large); clozapine vs. CNO: t(5) = 3.069, p=0.028, g=0.226(small))
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data with reference to Figure 2a-I.

claim: A significant increase in MVadjPerGram was observed within saline, clozapine and CNO injected hM3Dq animals.
source: (2) MVadjPerGram: (Figure 2a–VI; saline vs. clozapine: t(5) = –2.790, p=0.038, g=–0.974(large); saline vs. CNO: t(5) = –2.600, p=0.048, g = –0.928(large))
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data with reference to Figure 2a-VI.

claim: A significant increase in PIFadj was observed within saline, clozapine and CNO injected hM3Dq animals.
source: (3) PIFadj (Figure 2a–VII; saline vs. clozapine: t(5) = –2.726, p=0.041, g = –1.217(large); all reported results are post-hoc two-tailed paired student's t-Tests; g values represent the effect size according Hedge's g corrected for paired data, the magnitude of the effect size is provided in parentheses [i.e. negligible, small, medium, or large]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data with reference to Figure 2a-VII.

claim: The tidal volume normalized for bodyweight (TVadjPerGram) was not altered by the intervention.
source: Remarkably, the tidal volume normalized for bodyweight (TVadjPerGram; Figure 2a-IV) was not altered by the intervention (3x3 mixed-design ANOVA: F(2,26) = 1.165, p=0.322).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant effect, with reference to Figure 2a-IV.

claim: The principal factor explaining the changes in MVadjPerGram was the increased BPM.
source: Furthermore, since minute volume equals the tidal volume multiplied by BPM, it follows that, the principal factor explaining the changes in MVadjPerGram was the increased BPM.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between minute volume, tidal volume, and breathing rate.

claim: The inspiratory time (IT) decreased in hM3Dq animals following clozapine injection.
source: The inspiratory time (IT, Figure 2a–II; ; saline vs. clozapine: t(5) = 3.296, p=0.022, g=1.170[large])
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data with reference to Figure 2a-II.

claim: The total respiratory time (TT) decreased in hM3Dq animals following clozapine injection.
source: and the total respiratory time (TT, Figure 2a-IV; saline vs. clozapine:: t(5) = 2.683, p=0.043, g=1.140[large]) decreased
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data with reference to Figure 2a-IV.

claim: The expiratory time (ET) remained unaffected in hM3Dq animals.
source: while however the expiratory time (Figure 2a–III) remained unaffected (ET; mixed-design ANOVA: F(2,26) = 1.656, p=0.217).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant effect, with reference to Figure 2a-III.

claim: The increase in BPM was achieved by selectively shortening the IT through an increase in PIFadj.
source: Therefore, the increase in BPM was achieved by selectively shortening the IT through an increase in PIFadj, while expiratory parameters (e.g. PEFadj (Figure 2a–VIII)) did not achieve statistical significance level and therefore do not seem to have contributed significantly to the increase in BPM.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of changes in respiratory parameters.

claim: None of the respiratory parameters were altered to a level of statistical significance in the control group (DREADD_neg).
source: It is important to note that none of the parameters were altered to a level of statistical significance neither in the control group (DREADD_neg) nor in the inhibitory DREADD group (hM4Di).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of control group data.

claim: None of the respiratory parameters were altered to a level of statistical significance in the inhibitory DREADD group (hM4Di).
source: It is important to note that none of the parameters were altered to a level of statistical significance neither in the control group (DREADD_neg) nor in the inhibitory DREADD group (hM4Di).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of hM4Di group data.

claim: The effect on respiratory parameters was caused by neuronal excitation of the parvafoxFoxb1 and not by an inherent effect of the injected substances (i.e. clozapine or CNO).
source: This indicates that the effect was caused by neuronal excitation of the parvafoxFoxb1 and not by an inherent effect of the injected substances (i.e. clozapine or CNO).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of effects in control groups.

claim: The increase of c-Fos immunoreactivity was evident in the parvafox nucleus of hM3Dq expressing mice, but not in those of hM4Di expressing mice nor in control mice.
source: This conclusion is further strengthened by the increase of c-Fos immunoreactivity evident in the parvafox nucleus of hM3Dq expressing mice, but not in those of hM4Di expressing mice nor in control mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Global hM3Dq activation of the parvafoxFoxb1 decreased the distance moved to a level of statistical significance, however, with only a small effect size.
source: Global hM3Dq activation of the parvafoxFoxb1 decreased the distance moved to a level of statistical significance, however, with only a small effect size (t(4) = 3.774, p=0.02, g=0.225(small)).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of open field test data.

claim: The time spent in an immobile state was not affected by chemogenetic activation of the parvafoxFoxb1.
source: The time spent in an immobile state was not affected by chemogenetic activation of the parvafoxFoxb1 (t(4) = 2.257, p=0.087).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant effect.

claim: Activation of the inhibitory hM4Di receptors did not affect gross locomotor activity distance moved.
source: Activation of the inhibitory hM4Di receptors did not affect gross locomotor activity distance moved: t(4) = –0.697, p=0.524; time spent in immobile state: t(4) = 0.695, p=0.525.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant effect.

claim: Injections of clozapine in control mice (DREADD_neg) did not alter distance moved.
source: Injections of clozapine in control mice (DREADD_neg) did not alter distance moved (t(3) = –2.708, p=0.073)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant effect.

claim: Injections of clozapine in control mice (DREADD_neg) led to a statistically significant decrease of time spent in an immobile state, however, with a negligible effect size.
source: but lead to a statistically significant decrease of time spent in an immobile state, however, with a negligible effect size t(3) = 4.336, p=0.027, g=0.081 (negligible).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of control group data.

claim: The magnitude of the effect size of chemogenetic modulation of the parvafoxFoxb1 on gross locomotor activity is unlikely to explain the large size of the effects observed in the alterations of respiratory patterns.
source: Thus, despite reaching statistical significance for distance moved in hM3Dq animals and for time spent in an immobile state in DREADD_neg animals, the magnitude of the effect size of chemogenetic modulation of the parvafoxFoxb1 on gross locomotor activity is only small and negligible, respectively, and is unlikely to explain the large size of the effects observed in the alterations of respiratory patterns.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing effect sizes across different measures.

claim: ChR2-expressing mice exhibited a short-latency immobility response immediately after onset of the photostimulation with blue light.
source: These mice exhibited a short-latency immobility response immediately after onset of the photostimulation with blue light (7–15 mW, burst of 500ms duration with an intraburst frequency of 30 Hz (5ms pulse duration) and an interburst interval of 500ms).
evidence: This is a direct observation from optogenetic experiments.

claim: A decrease of locomotor activity was observed in 13 out of 16 ChR2-expressing mice.
source: A decrease of locomotor activity was observed in 13 out of 16 ChR2-expressing mice (Figure 3a–c), of which eight mice showed almost complete absence of locomotion.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from optogenetic experiments with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Eight ChR2-expressing mice showed almost complete absence of locomotion during photostimulation.
source: A decrease of locomotor activity was observed in 13 out of 16 ChR2-expressing mice (Figure 3a–c), of which eight mice showed almost complete absence of locomotion.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from optogenetic experiments with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Three ChR2-expressing mice were still capable of moving their heads as a sign of attentive behavior towards its surroundings while all four limbs remained largely immobile.
source: Three of these mice were still capable of moving their heads as a sign of attentive behavior towards its surroundings (158/19, 160/19, and 35B-20), while all four limbs remained largely immobile (Video 1).
evidence: This is a qualitative observation from optogenetic experiments with reference to Video 1.

claim: Five ChR2-expressing mice displayed complete immobility (including head activity) during almost the entire duration of the LEDon period.
source: Five other mice (162/19, 106/21–10, 34/21–7, 34/21–10, and 35E-20) displayed an even greater effect and remained completely immobile (including head activity) during almost the entire duration of the LEDon period (Video 2).
evidence: This is a qualitative observation from optogenetic experiments with reference to Video 2.

claim: No activity bursts were observed during or after the photostimulation period in ChR2-expressing mice.
source: No activity bursts were observed, neither during nor after the photostimulation period.
evidence: This is a negative observation from optogenetic experiments.

claim: Increasing the intensity of the stimulation from 70 to 222 mW using a laser beam did not trigger motor activities.
source: Increasing the intensity of the stimulation from 70 to 222 mW (measured at patchcord) using a laser beam did not trigger motor activities.
evidence: This is a negative observation from optogenetic experiments with increased stimulation intensity.

claim: Photoactivation in OnTarget_antPAG mice with ChR2 expression significantly decreased distance moved.
source: Two-tailed paired Welch's t-Tests revealed significant effects of photoactivation in the following parameters in OnTarget_antPAG mice with ChR2 expression in the ventral-posterior hypothalamus (Figure 3a–h): Distance moved (t(8) = 5.934, p<0.001, g=2.506 [large])
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of optogenetic experiment data with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Photoactivation in OnTarget_antPAG mice with ChR2 expression significantly decreased speed.moving.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of optogenetic experiment data.

claim: Photoactivation in OnTarget_antPAG mice with ChR2 expression significantly increased time in immobile state.
source: time in immobile state: (t(8) = –4.704, p=0.002, g = –1.976 [large])
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of optogenetic experiment data.

claim: Photoactivation in OnTarget_antPAG mice with ChR2 expression significantly decreased time in center.
source: time in center (t(8) = 4.108, p=0.003, g=1.178 [large])
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of optogenetic experiment data.

claim: Photoactivation in OnTarget_antPAG mice with ChR2 expression significantly increased time in periphery.
source: and time in periphery (t(8) = –2.841, p=0.022, g=–0.903 [large]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of optogenetic experiment data.

claim: Photoinhibition in ArchT3.0 OnTarget_antPAG mice consistently changed locomotor parameters in a direction opposite to the ChR2 mice.
source: Besides speed.moving: (t(3) = 0.096, p=0.929), photoinhibition in ArchT3.0 OnTarget_antPAG mice consistently changed locomotor parameters in a direction opposite to the ChR2 mice (Figure 3a–h): Distance moved (t(3) = –3.176, p=0.050, g = –0.832 [large]), time in immobile state: (t(3) = 5.369, p=0.013, g = –1.712 [large]), time in center (t(3) = –4.590, p=0.019, g = –0.885 [large]) and time in periphery (t(3) = 1.367, p=0.265).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of optogenetic inhibition experiments with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The large volume of virus injected (200 nl) and the highly penetrant and strongly expressing viral serotype of the vector used (AAV5) led to expression of ChR2 not only in the parvafoxFoxb1 neurons but also in other Foxb1-expressing hypothalamic neurons in the neighboring mammillary region.
source: A comment about the specificity of the optogenetic results: the large volume of virus injected (200 nl) and the highly penetrant and strongly expressing viral serotype of the vector used (AAV5) led to expression of ChR2 not only (as intended) in the parvafoxFoxb1 neurons but also in other Foxb1-expressing hypothalamic neurons in the neighboring mammillary region.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a technical limitation in the experimental design.

claim: Of all the mammillary nuclei only the dorsal premammillary nuclei (PMd) send axons to the rostral dlPAG.
source: However, of all the mammillary nuclei only the dorsal premammillary nuclei (PMd) send axons to the rostral dlPAG (Vertes, 1992; Meller and Dennis, 1986; Canteras and Swanson, 1992), where the tip of the glass fibers for the optogenetic activation were implanted.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: In the optogenetic experiments, the terminals from the PMdFoxb1 were co-activated with those of the parvafoxFoxb1.
source: In our experiments, the terminals from the PMdFoxb1 were therefore co-activated with those of the parvafoxFoxb1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical connectivity and the experimental design.

claim: Projections to the rostral dlPAG from other mamillary neurons are very scarce.
source: Projections to the rostral dlPAG from other mamillary neurons are very scarce (Allen and Hopkins, 1990; Shen, 1983; Beart et al., 1990; Cruce, 1977; Canteras et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: Optogenetic activation of Foxb1+ terminals originating from the hypothalamic parvafox nucleus and/or PMd and projecting to the anterior PAG induces a state of immobility and hypoactivity.
source: In summary, optogenetic activation of Foxb1+ terminals originating from the hypothalamic parvafox nucleus and/or PMd and projecting to the anterior PAG induces a state of immobility and hypoactivity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the optogenetic experimental data.

claim: Stimulation at more posterior positions along the PAG and/or ventral to the dlPAG columns are inefficient in inducing immobility behavior.
source: Stimulation at more posterior positions along the PAG and/or ventral to the dlPAG columns are inefficient in inducing this behavior.
evidence: This is an observation from optogenetic experiments comparing different stimulation sites.

claim: The observed effect of optogenetic activation is bidirectional, in the sense that inhibition of the same terminals in the anterior PAG induces increased distance moved, and time spent in the center of the arena, while decreasing the time spent in an immobile state.
source: The observed effect is bidirectional, in the sense that inhibition of the same terminals in the anterior PAG induces increased distance moved, and time spent in the center of the arena, while decreasing the time spent in an immobile state.
evidence: This is a summary of the bidirectional effects observed with activation vs. inhibition experiments.

claim: A cholecystokinin (Cck)-expressing population of neurons in the PMd has been shown to induce escape behavior in mice.
source: In contrast to this finding, a cholecystokinin (Cck)-expressing population of neurons in the PMd has been shown to induce escape behavior in mice (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Wang et al., 2021).

claim: The Cck-expressing and the Foxb1-expressing PMd neurons are distinct, separate neuronal groups regulating opposite behaviors.
source: We hypothesized that the Cck-expressing and the Foxb1-expressing PMd neurons are distinct, separate neuronal groups regulating opposite behaviors.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors based on their observations.

claim: K-nearest neighbor clustering resulted in 24 distinct cell types detected in the ventral-posterior hypothalamus.
source: After quality control, normalization, and integration of all four datasets (from two female and two male mice), k-nearest neighbor clustering resulted in 24 distinct cell types detected in the ventral-posterior hypothalamus (Figure 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing analysis with reference to Figure 4a.

claim: Cluster 9 was identified as the PMd based on expression of PMd markers.
source: Plotting the expression levels of a set of PMd markers identified by Mickelsen et al. (i.e. Cck, Foxb1, Synpr, Dlk1, Ebf3, and Stxbp6) onto the UMAP plot identified cluster 9 as the PMd (Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis with reference to Figure 4b.

claim: There are significantly higher expression levels of Cck than Foxb1 in the PMd cluster.
source: Plotting gene expression with fixed scales across both genes reveals significantly higher expression levels of Cck than Foxb1 in the PMd cluster (column d1 in Figure 4d).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis with reference to Figure 4d.

claim: Simultaneous visualization of both Cck and Foxb1 expression levels within the PMd cluster shows a biased expression pattern of Cck- and Foxb1-expressing cells towards opposing sides of the PMd cluster.
source: Simultaneous visualization of both Cck and Foxb1 expression levels within the PMd cluster shows a biased expression pattern of Cck- and Foxb1-expressing cells towards opposing sides of the PMd cluster (column d2 in Figure 4d).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression visualization with reference to Figure 4d.

claim: There is a substantial number of single-positive cells for each of Cck and Foxb1 in the PMd cluster.
source: There is a substantial number of single-positive cells for each of the two genes (column d3 in Figure 4d).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis with reference to Figure 4d.

claim: There is a group of PMd neurons co-expressing both Cck and Foxb1, but very few of them show high expression levels of both genes.
source: There is indeed a group of PMd neurons co-expressing both markers, but very few of them show high expression levels of both genes.
evidence: This is an observation from the single-cell RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: Although both Cck and Foxb1 are expressed throughout the entire PMd cluster, there are two well-defined, distinct, subpopulations of neurons expressing either Cck or Foxb1 but not both.
source: In summary, although both Cck and Foxb1 are expressed throughout the entire PMd cluster, there are two well-defined, distinct, subpopulations of neurons expressing either Cck or Foxb1 but not both.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the single-cell RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: The PMdFoxb1 is a novel subdivision of the PMd with functional distinction from the PMdCck.
source: We were hence able to introduce the presence of the PMdFoxb1 as a novel subdivision of the PMd with functional distinction from the PMdCck.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined anatomical, functional, and transcriptomic data.

claim: Two studies had previously identified the parvalbumin+ subpopulation of the parvafox nucleus (parvafoxPvalb) to be involved in nociceptive behaviors.
source: Two studies had previously identified the parvalbumin+ subpopulation of the parvafox nucleus (parvafoxPvalb) to be involved in nociceptive behaviors (Roccaro-Waldmeyer et al., 2018; Siemian et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: No significant difference was observed between BL and Stim conditions in any of the three tested animal groups in hot plate experiments.
source: In these experiments, we did not observe any significant difference between BL and Stim conditions in any of the three tested animal groups (Figure 5, ChR2-OnTarget_antPAG: Number of shakes before endpoint t(5) = –0.442, p=0.677 and latency until endpoint t(5) = 0.515, p=0.629; ChR-OffTarget: Number of shakes before endpoint t(10) = –1.076, p=0.307 and latency until endpoint t(10) = 1.716, p=0.117; ArchT3.0-OnTarget_antPAG: Number of shakes before endpoint t(5) = –0.344, p=0.753 and latency until endpoint z=1.150, p=0.875; all reported results are from Welch's t tests, except the last result that was obtained by a Wilcoxon signed-rank test due to non-normality of the data).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of hot plate test data with reference to Figure 5.

claim: The parvafoxFoxb1 does not exert a reciprocal effect on the parvafoxPvalb's role in pain sensation.
